metaTitle: Best Pit Boss Smokers in 2026, Ranked
metaDescription: Pit Boss pellet and gas smokers ranked by cooking area, controller, connectivity and sear ability, from a 256 sq in tabletop to a 1,539 sq in family rig.
expertTake: The Pit Boss 850 Navigator is the best model in the family for most households because it combines 932 sq in, WiFi and Bluetooth, and a flame broiler without the size of the 1600. The 500 FB2 is the value pick. Anyone cooking for one or two people on a tight budget should skip the big models and buy the 150.
introParagraphs: This brand sells mostly pellet smokers, plus a gas vertical, and the lineup is organized by cooking area and by how much electronics sit on top. The model number roughly tells you the size, and the series name tells you the controller and body.

Choosing well comes down to three decisions: how much grate you need, whether you want a phone connection and whether the sear lever matters. The right answer is usually in the middle of the family rather than at either end.

products.name: Pit Boss 850 Navigator WiFi and Bluetooth Pellet Grill and Smoker, 932 sq in
products.description:
The 850 Navigator offers 932 sq in of cooking surface, WiFi and Bluetooth control and an LCD digital controller. That is double the area of the 500 FB2 and enough to smoke a brisket and a rack of ribs side by side.

Its 180 to 500 F range covers low smoke, roasting and baking, and a flame broiler lever opens direct flame for searing. Having both WiFi and Bluetooth is a practical choice: Bluetooth keeps working close to the smoker when your home network does not reach the patio.

The downside is footprint and pellet use. A bigger body takes longer to preheat, and the pellet hopper needs refilling on long cooks. Keep pellets dry, vacuum the fire pot every few cooks and cover it between uses. Pair it by Bluetooth for the first test cook, then add WiFi once you trust the controller. Space ribs and a brisket on separate racks so the drippings do not mix, and give the first preheat a full fifteen minutes.
products.bestFor: Most households that want size, app control and a sear option.
pros: 932 sq in fits brisket and ribs together
WiFi plus Bluetooth for backup control
180 to 500 F range for all recipes
cons: Heavy and takes up patio space

products.name: Pit Boss 500 FB2 Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 518 sq in
products.description:
The 500 FB2 is the sweet spot for a family of four. Its 518 sq in is comfortable for two pork butts, and the LCD controller moves in 5 F steps across 180 to 500 F.

A flame broiler lever slides open a plate for direct-flame searing up to 1,000 F, which is the feature that makes this more than a plain smoker. It lacks the WiFi of the 850 Navigator, so you monitor at the control panel or with a separate thermometer.

It costs less than the connected models and is simple to maintain. Keep the hopper dry and the fire pot clean, and cover the cooker between cooks. The lever takes a minute to learn, so practice searing a thick steak before you rely on it for guests. A pellet cooker will never match the char of a charcoal sear, but 1,000 F on direct flame is close enough for most weeknight dinners.
products.bestFor: Families who want a capable smoker without paying for connectivity.
pros: 518 sq in suits a family of four
Flame broiler sears up to 1,000 F
cons: Timed controller drifts more than PID in wind

products.name: Pit Boss 700 Carbon Series Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 718 sq in
products.description:
The 700 Carbon fills the gap between the 500 FB2 at 518 sq in and the 850 Navigator at 932 sq in, with 718 sq in of cooking surface. It uses an LCD controller and the same 180 to 500 F range as its siblings.

The maker pitches the space as enough for dozens of patties at once, which is a helpful way to picture it. For smoking, it fits a pork butt or two, a couple of racks of ribs and a side dish. It lacks the WiFi of the Navigator models, so remote monitoring is limited.

It suits cooks who want more room than the entry model but are not looking for app control. Maintain it like any pellet cooker: dry pellets, a clean fire pot and a cover. Because it lacks an app, pair it with a wireless thermometer so you can watch the meat from the kitchen. Its extra grate makes it a good choice if you plan to batch cook on weekends and freeze portions.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want more grate than the 500 without WiFi.
pros: 718 sq in sits between the 500 and 850
LCD controller is simple to read
Lower complexity than the Navigator line
cons: Less area than the Navigator models

products.name: Pit Boss 440 Mahogany Series Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 518 sq in
products.description:
The 440 Mahogany is an older design with the same 518 sq in of space as the 500 FB2. It uses an LED digital controller rather than the LCD used on newer models, and its grates are porcelain-coated steel.

For most buyers it comes down to age and features. The newer 500 FB2 has an LCD with finer steps, and the 440 is a simpler panel. It still has the flame broiler, so it can sear as well as smoke.

It is a good value if you find it, and spare parts are easy to get because the design is long established. Store pellets dry, clean the pot and cover it between uses. Replacement grates and parts for this generation are easy to find, which is a real advantage when a part fails in year three. Its basic panel also means fewer electronics to age out.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the proven 518 sq in design.
pros: 518 sq in with a flame broiler

products.name: Pit Boss 1600 Navigator WiFi and Bluetooth Pellet Grill and Smoker, 1,539 sq in
products.description:
The 1600 Navigator is the largest cooker in the family, with 1,539 sq in of total cooking surface and a touchscreen controller. It matches the 850 on connectivity, with both WiFi and Bluetooth.

That much area suits a big family, a small catering job or a smoker-heavy holiday. The flame broiler and 180 to 500 F range carry over, so it grills as well as smokes.

It is oversized for a couple, burns more pellets than the smaller models and needs a good pad and a nearby outlet. Keep the cover on and the pellets dry. Pick the 850 instead unless you really cook for a crowd, since the extra grate area mostly turns into extra pellets burned.

products.name: Pit Boss 150 Portable Tabletop Pellet Grill and Smoker, 256 sq in
products.description:
The 150 is the portable model, a tabletop pellet smoker with 256 sq in of cooking surface. It has a latch-locking lid and two handles for carrying, and it shares the 180 to 500 F range of its larger siblings.

It suits camping, tailgating and small households. The space is small, so you will not fit a brisket, but a rack of ribs or a few chicken pieces fit fine.

It needs power, so plan for a battery pack or an outlet. It is cheap to run and easy to store. Pellet use is low because the burn pot is small, so a bag of pellets goes further than on the larger models. It also warms up faster, which suits a quick weeknight cook.

products.name: Pit Boss 3-Series Gas Vertical Smoker, 880 sq in
products.description:
The 3-Series is the family's propane vertical. It uses a dual-valve, dual-burner system rated at 12,500 BTU, and four racks add up to 880 sq in.

Its range of 100 to 320 F is wide on the low end, which makes it suitable for cold smoking and warm holds that the pellet models cannot manage. It does not reach pellet-grill temperatures for searing.

It needs no outlet, which makes it the Pit Boss to pick for a power-free patio. Check the hose each season and keep a spare tank. Wood chips do the flavoring, so use chunks in the chip box for longer smoke and refill every couple of hours on long cooks. It is a solid pick as a second smoker for cold smoking, even if you own a pellet unit.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want gas simplicity and a low temperature floor.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Match the model number to your household
buyingCriteria.explanation: The family runs from the 150 at 256 sq in through the 500 FB2 and 440 at 518 sq in, the 700 Carbon at 718 sq in and the 850 Navigator at 932 sq in to the 1600 Navigator at 1,539 sq in. A household of four needs roughly 400 to 500 sq in, so the 500 FB2 is the natural fit and the larger models are for groups. Plan for the pad as well: a flat, non-combustible surface at least a few feet from walls.

Only the Navigator models list WiFi and Bluetooth. The 500 FB2, 440 Mahogany and 700 Carbon use LCD or LED panels. If you run overnight cooks and want alerts on your phone, the Navigators are worth it. If you cook ribs on a weekend afternoon, you do not need it. A phone connection is also useful to check the smoker from a store or office on a rest day.

The flame broiler lever exposes direct flame for searing up to 1,000 F on the 500 FB2. Most pellet cookers cap at 450 to 500 F, so a flame broiler turns the smoker into a hot grill. The gas 3-Series has no such feature. Practice on thick steaks before the first dinner with guests.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Check the low end of the range
buyingCriteria.explanation: The pellet models start at 180 F, which suits smoking. The 3-Series gas model runs 100 to 320 F, which is the only one suited to cold smoking cheese or fish. If you cold smoke, look at the gas model. Many cooks keep the pellet model for flavor and add the gas smoker for cheese and fish.

The 440 Mahogany uses an LED digital controller, while newer models use an LCD with 5 F steps and the Navigators use a touchscreen or LCD. Newer controllers hold temperatures with finer steps. None are PID in the listings we have, so keep a separate thermometer. Fine control matters less than a stable body, so do not overpay for a screen.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Plan for pellet and pad needs
buyingCriteria.explanation: Larger bodies burn more pellets and take longer to preheat. The 1600 Navigator needs a big flat pad and a nearby outlet. Pellets must stay dry, and a cover is essential. Pellet cost adds up over a year, so factor that in when comparing sizes.

cards.label: Pellet
cards.text: The 500 FB2, 700 Carbon and Navigators burn real wood and reach 500 F, so they smoke, roast and sear. They need an outlet and dry pellets.

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The 3-Series runs on propane and goes down to 100 F for cold smoking. It needs no outlet but cannot sear.

howToChoose.note: Pick pellet for flavor and versatility, gas for simplicity and cold smoke.

howToChoose.subheading: For Searing and Smoking Together Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A flame broiler lever, a ceiling of 500 F and enough grate to separate hot and cool zones.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 500 FB2 and 850 Navigator both have the flame broiler and the range. The 850 adds more grate and app control.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook for groups or want remote alerts. The 850 and 1600 Navigator reward that.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook for a small household. The 150 or 500 FB2 is enough.

maintenance.why: Ash chokes airflow and causes flameouts. Check the igniter hole is clear.
Fat builds up and can ignite at high heat. Replace liners regularly.
On the 3-Series, cracked hoses leak gas. Brush soapy water on connections.
Damp pellets swell and jam the auger. Use a sealed bin.
Rain damages electronics and rusts steel.

faq.q: Which Pit Boss is best for a family?
faq.a: The 500 FB2 is the sensible pick for a family of four, with 518 sq in and a flame broiler. The 850 Navigator is better if you want app control. If budget is tight, the 440 Mahogany is often a similar size for less.

faq.q: Do Pit Boss pellet smokers need WiFi?
faq.a: No. Only the Navigator models list WiFi and Bluetooth. The others work from a control panel. Use a probe thermometer for the meat regardless of model.
The flame broiler models can reach direct flame up to 1,000 F on the 500 FB2. The gas 3-Series cannot. Preheat the broiler zone for a few minutes before the steak goes on.

faq.q: Which is best for cold smoking?
faq.a: The gas 3-Series runs as low as 100 F. The pellet models start at 180 F. Use cold smoke only in cool weather to keep cheese from melting.

faq.q: How much does a pellet cooker use?
faq.a: It depends on temperature, size and weather. Larger bodies and cold wind burn more pellets. As a rough rule, a hopper of pellets lasts many hours at smoking temperatures and far fewer at high heat.
For one or two people, yes. It holds a rack of ribs or a few chicken pieces, but not a brisket. It is also the cheapest way into pellet smoking.
